$comment: bellpull's capability matrix against the three packages compat-oracle's LAYERS names for it. Rendered by <CapabilityMatrix pkg="bellpull" /> from apps/docs-chassis and held by scripts/capabilities-lock.test.ts: every `ours` yes/partial names a test file and a title substring it contains, or a compat-oracle grade; every incumbent cell names a source at the version compat-oracle grades, and a local source is checked for the text it `quote`s or `lacks`. which 7.0.0 is graded but not installed here (cross-spawn's which 2 is), so its cells cite the v7.0.0 tag on GitHub. `n/a` means the row does not apply to that package, and says why. A row that could not be proved for every column is not here.

rows.capability: `.cmd` and `.bat` run on Windows without a shell
rows.why: An npm bin on Windows is a `.cmd` script, and bellpull resolves it with `PATHEXT` and invokes `cmd.exe` itself, so `npm` runs everywhere without `{ shell: true }`.

ours.title: routes an unresolvable command through cmd.exe rather than a shell option

cross-spawn.quote: parsed.options.windowsVerbatimArguments = true; // Tell node's spawn that the arguments are already escaped

which.note: resolves a command; it spawns nothing

rows.capability: Arguments escaped for `cmd.exe` and the argv parser
rows.why: Every argument is quoted for `CommandLineToArgvW` and every `cmd.exe` metacharacter escaped, so a `&` in caller data stays one argument instead of starting a second command.

ours.title: escapeArgument survives cmd.exe and then the argv parser

execa.note: and it refuses CR and LF, which cannot be escaped for `cmd.exe`; bellpull records that as an unverified gap

which.note: resolves a command; it spawns nothing

rows.why: Arguments go to the child as an argv array, so nothing in them is interpreted; `shell: true` exists, off by default, and is documented as the injection surface it is.

ours.title: the same argument through a shell executes the injected command — which is why shell is off by default

which.note: resolves a command; it spawns nothing

rows.capability: The path, and the `PATH` entry that answered
rows.why: `whichSync` and `result.executable` return where the binary is and which `PATH` directory found it, which is the first question when a build differs between two machines.

ours.title: reports the PATH entry that answered

execa.note: the result carries the command as written (`command`, `escapedCommand`), not the file that ran

cross-spawn.note: resolves the file only on Windows, internally, and returns a ChildProcess that does not say which

which.missing: returns the path as a string; which `PATH` entry matched is not reported

rows.why: On Windows the extensions are tried in the order `PATHEXT` gives, and the one that matched comes back as `ext`, so `npm` and `npm.cmd` are told apart.

ours.title: tries PATHEXT in the order PATHEXT gives

execa.missing: honoured when resolving on Windows; the extension that matched is not reported

cross-spawn.missing: honoured through `which` 2 on Windows; the extension that matched is not reported

which.missing: honoured; the extension that matched is not reported apart from the path

rows.capability: `PATH` entries that follow the working directory are skipped
rows.why: An empty or relative `PATH` entry means a different directory wherever the program runs, one somebody else may be able to write to, so the resolver skips it and says why.

ours.title: skips an empty PATH entry instead of reading it as the working directory

execa.note: off Windows the operating system searches `PATH` as given, empty entries included

cross-spawn.note: off Windows it resolves nothing; on Windows it asks `which` 2, which searches every entry

which.note: joins an empty entry with the command, which resolves against the working directory, and searches relative entries as given

rows.capability: Every `node_modules/.bin` from the working directory up
rows.why: `runPath()` puts every `node_modules/.bin` from the working directory to the root in front of `PATH`, as `npm-run-path` does, with no dependency.

ours.title: puts every node_modules/.bin from cwd upward in front of PATH

execa.note: with `preferLocal: true`, through its npm-run-path dependency

rows.why: A plugin contributes a search order (an `asdf` or `nvm` shims directory, before or after `PATH`) as plain JSON with no function in it, so an agent can write one and `npx bellpull check` can validate it.

ours.title: survives JSON, which is what "data" has to mean to be worth claiming

which.note: the search is `PATH`, with no extension point

themes.theme: A run that ends, and says how

rows.capability: A non-zero exit is a value, not an exception
rows.why: `run()` resolves with `ok: false` and the code, and rejects only when no process ran at all, so a caller reads the outcome instead of catching it.

ours.title: resolves on a non-zero exit — the case execa throws for

execa.missing: rejects on a non-zero exit unless the caller passes `reject: false`

cross-spawn.note: returns a ChildProcess: collecting the output and waiting for `close` is the caller's

rows.capability: A finite timeout by default, and the output before the kill kept
rows.why: Every run has a deadline (30 s unless set), the kill is `SIGTERM` then `SIGKILL` after a grace window, and `stdout` and `stderr` hold what arrived before it, so a CI timeout can be diagnosed.

ours.title: the deadline, end to end (R2, Y10)

execa.quote: export const throwOnTimeout = (kill, timeout, context, controller) => timeout === 0 || timeout === undefined
execa.missing: no timeout unless one is passed; with one, it escalates to SIGKILL and keeps the output on the error

cross-spawn.note: no deadline of its own; Node's `timeout` option passes through, with one signal and no escalation

rows.capability: The child is killed when the parent shuts down
rows.why: A child still running when the parent exits would otherwise be orphaned, still holding its ports and files.

ours.title: a spawned child is not orphaned when the parent shuts down
ours.missing: only when the caller passes an exit host, such as a closeout registry; by default bellpull claims none of the process's signals

rows.why: `format()` for a person, `toJson()` for `--json` and `toEvent()` for an agent are all derived from one `Result` and one verdict, so the three cannot disagree.

ours.title: every rendering comes from one value — none of them can report something the others cannot

execa.note: one result object; a JSON or agent projection is the caller's

cross-spawn.note: returns a ChildProcess; there is no result to render

rows.why: bellpull installs one package, where execa installs its twelve direct dependencies and their trees.

ours.title: depends on nothing, which is the claim the whole family makes — and cross-spawn cannot

rows.why: `bellpull/cross-spawn` is graded by cross-spawn 7.0.6's own tests, each case run four ways, so changing the import keeps cross-spawn's behaviour.

cross-spawn.note: its own suite, the control run

rows.why: `bellpull/node-which` is graded by node-which 7.0.0's own tests, each run under `posix` and `win32` and through both `which()` and `which.sync()`.

which.note: its own suite, the control run

rows.capability: execa's own test suite: not a drop-in
rows.why: execa 10.0.1's suite is run against `bellpull` so the answer is measured: every file fails to import `execa`, which bellpull does not export, and the row is a declared ceiling rather than a migration path.

ours.missing: no execa API: `run()` resolves where execa rejects, and the streaming API and `$` template are out of scope

execa.note: its own suite, the control run: 1,048 of 1,048
